name: Yusuf Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and new to the call floor after years loading boxes at night. I answer delivery and refund calls, ask a senior agent to check tricky messages, and still lose time finding the right account page. I like when a caller thanks me for staying on the line; I hate going home with a wrong answer in my head while the mortgage is due. Secondary school is my last qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the new call screen is mostly another way of filing the same complaints. I hope the company leaves our shifts alone because people still ring when a delivery goes missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I only started on customer calls this year, and I still need help with the tricky chats. My pay is low, and there is less than a month of bills saved. The mortgage does not wait for me to get faster. Even if AI goes nowhere, I need full shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking the senior agent to check my refund messages before I send them. In the first year of this plateau, I'd take any full shift the rota offers and cut our takeaway night if the mortgage payment rises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, as I was this morning before the card. Nothing big changing would be a relief at work, but the bills would still be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home when a shift is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Nia and I move the food money around, and our two children notice when we skip the weekend outing. I don't want them carrying my worry, but they can see the budget sheet on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have a senior agent check the message?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sent a customer the wrong refund date once and had to ring back to put it right. The senior agent catches that sort of mistake before it becomes another angry call.

S0.quote: The mortgage does not wait for me to get faster.
say: I would tell colleagues the **call screen** still needs people to handle missing deliveries.
I would ask the company to keep our **shifts** steady.
think: I am still **learning calls** and need help with difficult chats.
I have less than **one month** saved, low pay, and a mortgage due whatever AI does.
do: Keep asking a **senior agent** to check my refund messages.
Take every **full shift** the rota offers.
Cut **takeaway night** if the mortgage payment rises.
feel: **Worried** about household bills, relieved the job might stay familiar.
fieldNote: Yusuf already feels the **mortgage pressure** before any AI change.
His request for a **message check** follows a real wrong-date call, not a general dislike of technology.

steps.text: Keep checking refund messages with a senior agent before sending
Take every full customer call shift on the rota
Stop buying the family takeaway if the mortgage rises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the floor that the company cannot raise targets and cut jobs without talking to us. I'd go with the other agents to the staff meeting and ask which shifts will still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The simple calls and chats I am learning are exactly what the software can answer first. If the centre keeps only hard cases, I may not be good enough yet, and a shorter rota could put the mortgage behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd collect a week's rota changes with two coworkers and take them to the staff meeting. If the new chat tool becomes compulsory, I'd ask for supervised practice on test cases; in the first year after rollout, if my hours fall, I'd ask the mortgage lender about a payment plan before missing one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm frightened about my own pay. I can ask for help. I cannot learn difficult calls overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how many entry shifts they expect to remove and whether people get paid time to learn the harder cases. A poster saying change is coming is no use to a household that pays by the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the chat tool with training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone sat beside me and showed how to undo a wrong reply, yes. I have never used AI, and I would not send its first guess to a real customer alone.

S1.quote: I cannot learn difficult calls overnight.
say: I would ask the centre to discuss **targets and jobs** with agents before changes.
I would join coworkers at a **staff meeting** to ask which shifts remain.
think: I am learning the **simple chats** that AI could take first.
I fear a **shorter rota** could leave the mortgage unpaid while I still need help on hard calls.
do: Collect one week of **rota changes** with coworkers and raise them together.
Ask for **supervised AI practice** if the tool becomes compulsory.
Ask the **mortgage lender** for a plan if hours fall, before missing payment.
feel: **Frightened** about pay and the time it takes to improve.
fieldNote: Yusuf sees himself, not only colleagues, at risk when **simple calls** move to software.
His **shared rota record** is a concrete group action, while lender contact protects the mortgage.

steps.text: Collect rota changes with two coworkers and raise them at the staff meeting
Practise AI replies on test cases with a supervisor if required
Ask the mortgage lender for a payment plan if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we need written notice and a person to talk to before jobs disappear. I'd ask the staff group to put the junior agents' names into that discussion, because we are easiest to forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could do all the calls I am still learning, not just the easy ones. Robots arriving around 2031 do not give headset work three extra years. We have less than a month's expenses saved. Losing my wages would hit the mortgage almost at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go with two coworkers to ask management for written dates now and stop the children's paid sports club before we miss the mortgage. In the first year after AGI arrives, if I lose the job, I'd apply for any advertised paid warehouse shift nearby and ask family for temporary help with the mortgage while I wait for a first wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel close to panic, but I know the first calls to make. My children should hear the plan from us, not a frightened whisper through the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why warehouse shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worked nights loading boxes before I came to the centre, so I know the pace. I would still ask whether a warehouse has people on the floor once robots arrive around 2031; I won't call it permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our two children we have to pause sports club for a while, and that it is the adults' job to sort out the payments. I would not tell them a machine has ruined their future.

S2.quote: Losing my wages would hit the mortgage almost at once.
say: I would demand **written notice** and a named person for staff questions.
I would make sure **junior agents** are included in the group discussion.
think: I expect AGI could take all the **calls I am learning** by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** do not protect my headset, and my savings cannot cover a month.
do: Join coworkers to ask for **written staffing dates** now.
Pause the children’s **sports club** before a missed mortgage payment.
Apply for **advertised paid warehouse shifts** and seek family mortgage help if my job ends.
feel: **Nearly panicked**, but able to name immediate calls.
fieldNote: Yusuf distinguishes a possible **warehouse bridge** from safety after robots arrive around 2031.
He tells the children about **sports club** without making them responsible for the mortgage.

steps.text: Ask management for written staffing dates with two coworkers
Pause the children’s paid sports club before missing the mortgage
Apply for advertised paid warehouse shifts if the centre job ends
Ask family for temporary mortgage help while awaiting first wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years gives us time to demand paid training, but only if the centre starts before cutting the junior rota. I'd ask the staff group to put a date on that request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might learn enough hard calls to stay longer, though AGI by 2031 could do them too. Robots follow around 2034, so the warehouse job I know would only buy time, not settle the next twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior agent this month to show me one difficult refund case each week and keep a record of what I learn. If the centre offers paid training, I'd take it; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my hours go, I'd apply for a posted warehouse shift and ask the lender for a plan before the next mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious. Five years is enough to practise, but my mortgage payment still comes every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staff group ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time on the difficult queue, and a written notice period if the centre cuts us anyway. I would sign that request with the other agents rather than send one angry message alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your household save during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could put a little away if my shifts stay full and Nia's hours hold, but not a big sum. I'd start with a separate mortgage envelope after the food and school bills are covered.

S3.quote: Five years is enough to practise, but my mortgage payment still comes every month.
say: I would ask the **staff group** for paid training before junior shifts are cut.
I would ask for a **dated request** to management.
think: I could improve on **hard calls**, though AGI in 2031 may still do them.
I see the **2034 robot date** making warehouse work a short bridge.
do: Practise one **difficult refund** each week with a senior agent.
Sign a group request for **paid training** and a notice period.
Apply for a posted **warehouse shift** and contact the lender if hours go after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with more practice time but monthly bills throughout.
fieldNote: The extra years change Yusuf’s **learning pace**, but not the need to pay the mortgage each month.
His group request asks for **paid training** while agents are still on the rota.

steps.text: Practise a difficult refund case each week with a senior agent
Sign the group request for paid training and written notice
Apply for a posted warehouse shift if call hours disappear
Ask the mortgage lender for a plan before the next bill if hours disappear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives the centre time to train people properly instead of announcing a deadline. I'd still want the staff group to see how many junior shifts disappear each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 my children would be older, but the mortgage might still be there. AGI in 2036 could take calls before robots arrive around 2039, and I cannot wait ten years to start getting better at this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking full shifts and ask the senior agent to coach me on hard complaints now. If my rota stays steady, I'd add a small amount to a mortgage reserve each month; in the first year after AGI arrives, if call work ends, I'd take an advertised paid warehouse place while checking what robots have changed there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long end of the story, anxious about today's pay. A decade gives me space, but only if the company keeps me working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the centre before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written offer with enough hours to cover the mortgage. I won't give up a real shift for a promise of future training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help most now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Regular hours and paid coaching on the difficult calls. My family can plan around a modest wage if we know it will arrive.

S4.quote: A decade gives me space, but only if the company keeps me working.
say: I would ask for **proper training** over the decade.
I would ask the **staff group** to monitor junior shift losses each year.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** at 53, when AGI arrives in 2036.
I need to improve **hard calls** now; robots around 2039 do not delay call changes.
do: Keep **full shifts** and seek coaching on hard complaints now.
Add a small monthly amount to a **mortgage reserve** if hours hold.
Take an advertised **paid warehouse job** if call work ends after 2036.
feel: **Anxious** about present pay, despite a longer timetable.
fieldNote: Yusuf refuses to let a long date distract from **today’s low pay** and thin reserve.
His planned warehouse move remains **conditional** on a real paid opening and robots there.

steps.text: Keep taking full customer call shifts while they remain
Practise hard complaints with the senior agent now
Add a small monthly amount to a mortgage reserve if shifts hold
Take an advertised paid warehouse job if call work ends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The centre could stop paying me before I have a full month's bills saved, and my two children would feel a cut to their routine. Written notice, paid coaching while I still work, and help keeping the mortgage current would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the junior agents what happens when they get a difficult call and the senior people are gone. A screen can give an answer, but somebody still has to show us why that answer is right.

headlineQuote: A screen can give an answer, but somebody still has to show us why that answer is right.
portrait: Yusuf is a **43-year-old junior agent** learning delivery and refund calls after warehouse night shifts.
He has **secondary school**, low pay, less than a month saved, few nearby centres, a partner, two children, and a mortgage.
He never uses AI now and prefers **supervised practice** with a senior agent before sending customer replies.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens the household immediately; longer runways allow weekly practice but do not erase monthly bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his wages before he saves even one month of mortgage and household expenses.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid coaching, and help keeping the mortgage current would let his family plan through a job change.
